rv.q: Tom Stoppard's 'Arcadia' is arguably the finest play by a living dramatist, a work that manages to be simultaneously profound and entertaining, intellectually rigorous and emotionally satisfying.
Arcadia, back on Broadway for the first time since 1995, is a heady, aching thrill of a tragicomedy.
Watching David Leveaux’s production I realized more than ever that “Arcadia,” a tale of two centuries in pseudopastoral England, is propelled by genuine, panting passion.
On this level alone, the play is an enchantment.
Seldom has a more romantic finale been more rationally, stealthily staged–the impact sneaks up on you.
That’s too infrequently the case with this uneven cast.
It's easy to admire, but hard to love.
She raves “the acting could hardly be better … personally I preferred this cast to the original production’s” and gives it an A-.
This production of Arcadia succeeds because it finds the perfect balance between Stoppard's intellectual complexity and his emotional accessibility.
It may be Stoppard's best play, and even an indistinct production can't subdue its poignancy and wisdom.

tn.cat: Best Featured Actor in a Play

cn.t: Critics mostly praise Stoppard's intellectually dazzling masterpiece, though some find Leveaux's revival emotionally muted. The production balances complex ideas with heart, but execution proves uneven despite strong individual performances.

vs.sum: The Ethel Barrymore Theatre offers good sightlines with a well-raked mezzanine and minimal obstructions, though some box seats have limited views. Sound quality is average, with some reports of less than ideal acoustics. Comfort is typical for a Broadway theater, with decent legroom in some areas. However, facilities are lacking, with only one restroom on the lower level leading to potential congestion.

acc.note: 5 wheelchair spaces in Orchestra. No steps from sidewalk. Infrared devices available.
